subject: Tail latency composition and cold-start recovery — benchmarking questionnaire
summary: Globex requested a detailed breakdown of tail-latency composition and articulation of cold-start/cold-cache recovery methodology. Redwood proposed a two-stage benchmark (ramp + spike), provided a runbook and a spreadsheet for their telemetry, and asked clarifying questions about target sequence lengths, batching modes, and acceptable QoS thresholds. Final message confirms scheduling for an instrumented run and next steps for log uploads.
messages:
From: Alex Morgan <alex.morgan@globex.com>
To: Lauren Bishop <lauren_bishop@redwood.com>
Cc: ops+procurement@globex.com
Date: 2026-09-19T09:12:00-07:00
Subject: Performance questionnaire: tail-latency composition + cold-start recovery

Hi Lauren,

Thanks for taking the time. As part of our RFP evaluation we'd like a focused questionnaire and evidence around two areas: (1) tail-latency composition (we care about 95/99/99.9 breakdowns into model compute vs kernel/IO vs queuing), and (2) cold-start / cold-cache recovery behavior (how quickly KV/prefix caches warm, and what happens to p99/p99.9 during warm-up and immediate burst scenarios).

What we need from Redwood:
- A clear definition of how you measure component-level latency (wall-clock breakdown) and a short example trace.
- Typical p95/p99/p99.9 numbers for a 7B-ish model family on your hosted fleet and for Dedicated (per-GPU reserved) under our target configs (see below).
- Protocol for synthetic runs vs replayed production traces — pros/cons and recommended approach for repeatability.
- A recommended benchmark plan we can run together (automation, required artifacts, pass/fail criteria).
- Any constraints for quantized models / kernel fallbacks and how they affect tail behavior.

Our target config for the test: 128-length tokens average, 2048 max, 16-token generation windows, burst to 400 concurrent requests for 30s, sustained 80 qps for 15m. We expect you to say what you will measure and what telemetry we should provide.

If you can provide a short runbook and a spreadsheet we can populate with our traces, that would be ideal.

Thanks,
Alex Morgan
Lead SRE, Globex Corp

P.S. Please CC product security if you intend to share any internal run logs; procurement will need a digestible artifact for our evaluation committee.
From: Lauren Bishop <lauren_bishop@redwood.com>
To: Alex Morgan <alex.morgan@globex.com>
Cc: karthik_iyer@redwood.com, marissa_cole@redwood.com, dev_patel@redwood.com
Date: 2026-09-19T11:04:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Performance questionnaire: tail-latency composition + cold-start recovery

Alex —

Appreciate the clear ask. We've put together a targeted runbook and a spreadsheet template (attached) that will let us map telemetry to component-level buckets. Quick notes up front:

1) Measurement approach
- Wall-clock breakdown: client submit -> network ingress -> router queuing -> runtime dispatch -> model compute -> serialization/egress. We instrument at RPC boundary and inside the runtime to attribute time to each bucket.
- For p99.9 stability we recommend end-to-end sampling at 10s resolution plus full-trace captures for anomalous windows.

2) Configs & expected baselines (illustrative on Redwood-hosted C-profile GPUs, non-quantized):
- p95: ~18–24 ms
- p99: ~35–55 ms
- p99.9: ~80–150 ms (heavily workload dependent; tails driven by cache misses and kernel fallback).

3) Cold-start / cache warm-up behavior
- Prefix/KV cache: warm-up is exponential with the effective working set. With replayed traces we typically see 70–90% hit-rate within first 60s for steady prefixes; worst-case cold start for previously unseen long prefixes can push p99.9 to 400–700 ms until warmed.

4) Synthetic vs replayed traces
- Synthetic: easy to reproduce, useful for stress tests (ramp/spike).
- Replayed: best for real impacts on KV/prefix cache heat maps. We recommend running both: synthetic for controlled SLO validation, replayed for realistic tail exploration.

Next steps: We attached a runbook (benchmark-runbook-v1.pdf) and a sheet (tail_latency_breakdown_template.xlsx) with columns for trace ids, seq len, kv_hit, kernel_path, observed buckets. KarTHIK / Dev — can you add a short appendix explaining our kernel-fallback taxonomy and the recommended lab runs?

Scheduling: Alex, are you available next Tuesday (2026-09-22) for an instrumented run (we can provision a dedicated pool for 2 hours)?

— Lauren
Lauren Bishop
Sr. Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
lauren_bishop@redwood.com | +1 415 555 0129

From: Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.com>
To: Alex Morgan <alex.morgan@globex.com>
Cc: Lauren Bishop <lauren_bishop@redwood.com>, marissa_cole@redwood.com, dev_patel@redwood.com
Date: 2026-09-20T08:22:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Performance questionnaire: tail-latency composition + cold-start recovery

Alex — quick technical appendix attached inline below and some initial numbers from our internal microbench pool. Attaching sample KV warmup logs (kv_cache_warmup_logs_sample.tar.gz) that show per-key insert and hit-rate over time.

--- Attachment: kv_cache_warmup_logs_sample.tar.gz (sample logs, gzipped text) ---

High-level notes:
- Kernel fallback taxonomy: fast path (fmha-optimized kernels) vs slower generic kernels when attention patterns or kv sizes exceed optimized codepaths; fallback probability increases with sequence length and when quantized kernels are not available for a particular op.
- Observed microbench (Redwood-hosted, 8xA100-simulated config for a 7B model emulation):
  - single-request median model compute: 12 ms
  - single-request p99 model compute: 28 ms
  - serialization/egress median: 1.5 ms
  - queuing contribution under 400 concurrent uniform load: typically 5–30 ms depending on batching policy

Proposed lab runs (what we'll execute during the dedicated 2hr window):
1) Ramp test (replay): start from cold (empty caches), ramp to 80 qps over 10m, hold for 15m — measure hit-rate curves by prefix length and p95/p99/p99.9 progression.
2) Spike test (synthetic burst): keep working set warm at 80 qps, then inject a 30s burst to 400 concurrency — capture tail behavior and failover routing metrics.
3) Isolation runs: verify quantized model path vs FP16 path to show kernel-fallback impact.

Instrumentation we need from Globex: a sample of 10k request traces (request_id, timestamp, prompt_len, prefix_hash if allowed, kv_hit boolean if you already capture) and desired QoS thresholds (i.e., acceptable p99.9 in ms). If you can't share prefix content, a hashed prefix id column will suffice.

— Karthik (on behalf of runtime team)
Karthik Iyer
Principal Software Engineer, Redwood Inference

From: Dev Patel <dev_patel@redwood.com>

Date: 2026-09-21T10:16:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Performance questionnaire: tail-latency composition + cold-start recovery

Alex — adding a couple concrete examples from recent runs to set expectations. Quick paste of two representative windows (numbers rounded):

Example A (cold start window, synthetic replay, 128 avg len):
- t=0–30s: p95 32 ms, p99 78 ms, p99.9 420 ms (KV hit-rate ramping 0% -> 65%)
- t=30–120s: p95 22 ms, p99 46 ms, p99.9 110 ms (KV hit-rate stabilized ~85%)

Example B (warm steady-state, burst to 400 concurrent):
- baseline (80 qps): p95 20 ms, p99 40 ms, p99.9 95 ms
- burst window (peak): p95 24 ms, p99 60 ms, p99.9 210–260 ms (queuing + occasional fallback to generic kernel)

We will also export per-token compute-time histograms and the router queue length over time. For the run we propose the following pass/fail thresholds (example):
- p99.9 sustained under 250 ms during burst (pass for our dedicated pool)
- no more than 0.5% requests exceeding 500 ms outside of identified cache-warmup windows

If Globex has stricter numbers, please tell us up front and we'll tune the lab configuration or recommend dedicated capacity specs.

— Dev
Dev Patel
Performance Engineer, Redwood Inference

From: Alex Morgan <alex.morgan@globex.com>

Thanks Lauren, Karthik, Dev — this is exactly the level of detail we needed. We reviewed the proposed runs and thresholds with our SRE lead. A few confirmations:
- We'll provide anonymized replay traces (10k) including hashed prefixes and request metadata by EOD Monday (2026-09-27).
- We accept the two-stage runbook. Please provision the dedicated pool on 2026-09-29 10:00–12:00 PT.
- Our target pass threshold for the RFP is p99.9 < 300 ms during the burst window; anything above that will need an engineering mitigation plan documented.

Please include a short executive summary in the run artifacts (one page) we can circulate to our procurement committee. We'll upload any supporting telemetry to the shared S3 link (we'll provide credentials).

Appreciate the quick turnaround — looking forward to the instrumented run.

Alex Morgan
Lead SRE, Globex Corp
